items.followUp: How does mitosis help a cut or wound heal?

rubric.why: Mitosis produces new body cells with the same genetic information as the original cell.
rubric.description: States that mitosis produces cells identical to the original cell.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the new cells as genetically or otherwise identical.

rubric.why: The new cells replace body cells that are worn out or damaged.
rubric.description: Explains that new cells replace worn-out or damaged cells or help repair tissues.
rubric.how: Award for linking mitosis to cell replacement or tissue repair.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells that are genetically identical to the original cell.
These cells replace worn-out or damaged body cells and help repair tissues.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis when temperature rises above its optimum?

rubric.why: As temperature rises, enzyme-controlled reactions generally speed up until they reach an optimum temperature.
rubric.description: States that the rate of photosynthesis increases up to an optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award for describing the increase in rate before the optimum.

rubric.why: Above the optimum, photosynthetic enzymes denature and the rate falls.
rubric.description: States that the rate decreases above the optimum, due to enzyme denaturation.
rubric.how: Award for the decrease above the optimum; require enzyme denaturation for the cause-based alternative.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of photosynthesis increases up to an optimum because the reactions are enzyme-controlled.
Above the optimum, enzymes denature and the rate of photosynthesis decreases.

items.followUp: Where in the cell does the electron transport chain occur, and what does it produce?

rubric.why: Energy is released at several stages of respiration, not exclusively in the electron transport chain.
rubric.description: Explains that energy release occurs throughout respiration and not only in the electron transport chain.
rubric.how: Award for clearly rejecting the idea that the electron transport chain is the only energy-releasing step.

rubric.why: In the electron transport chain, electrons pass between carriers and the released energy is used to make ATP.
rubric.description: Describes electron transfer through carriers or its role in ATP production.
rubric.how: Award for an accurate description of the electron transport chain or its role in ATP production.

modelAnswer: Energy is released in stages throughout respiration, so it is incorrect to say that it is released only in the electron transport chain.
In the electron transport chain, electrons pass along carriers, and the released energy is used to make ATP.

items.followUp: Which enzymes in biological detergents help remove protein and fat stains?

rubric.why: Enzymes break down biological substances in stains so they can be removed during washing.
rubric.description: Explains how enzymes help biological detergents remove stains.
rubric.how: Award for stating that enzymes break down or remove biological stains.

rubric.why: Different detergent enzymes act on particular substances, such as proteins, fats or starch.
rubric.description: Gives a correct enzyme and the type of stain it breaks down.
rubric.how: Award for a correct enzyme-substrate example.

modelAnswer: Biological detergents contain enzymes that break down organic substances in stains, helping remove them during washing.
For example, proteases break down protein stains, and lipases break down fat stains.

items.followUp: What happens to the reaction rate when all enzyme active sites are occupied?

rubric.why: An enzyme is saturated when substrate molecules occupy all its active sites.
rubric.description: Defines saturation as all enzyme active sites being occupied by substrate.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the enzyme's active sites are all filled or occupied.

accept: more substrate does not increase the rate
rubric.why: When all active sites are occupied, the enzyme is working at its maximum rate; extra substrate cannot increase the rate.
rubric.description: States the effect of saturation on reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award for noting that the rate is maximum or will not rise when more substrate is added.

modelAnswer: Saturation of active sites means that substrate molecules are occupying all the active sites of the enzymes.
The reaction is then at its maximum rate, so adding more substrate does not increase the rate.

items.followUp: How does the lock-and-key model explain enzyme specificity?

rubric.why: The model explains enzyme specificity by the particular fit between an enzyme's active site and its substrate.
rubric.description: States that an enzyme's active site has a specific shape that fits its substrate.
rubric.how: Award for describing the specific shape match between active site and substrate.

rubric.why: When the substrate binds to the active site, an enzyme-substrate complex forms and products can be released.
rubric.description: Describes binding or complex formation in the lock-and-key model.
rubric.how: Award for stating that substrate binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex or leads to product release.

modelAnswer: The lock-and-key model states that an enzyme's active site has a specific shape that fits its substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
The substrate binds to form an enzyme-substrate complex, and products are released.

items.followUp: How does transpiration pull help water move up through xylem?

rubric.why: Transpiration from leaves creates tension that pulls water upward through the xylem.
rubric.description: States that transpiration creates tension or a pull in the xylem.
rubric.how: Award for identifying transpiration as the source of the upward pulling force.

rubric.why: Cohesion between water molecules keeps the water column continuous as it is pulled upward.
rubric.description: Explains how cohesion maintains the water column.
rubric.how: Award for linking cohesion to a continuous water column.

modelAnswer: The cohesion-tension theory states that transpiration from leaves creates tension in the xylem, pulling water upward.
Cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous column of water from the roots to the leaves.
